title: Classes bundle data with behaviour
explanation:
A **class** is a blueprint; calling it (`Point(1, 2)`) creates an **instance**. If the class defines `__init__`, Python calls it automatically on the new instance so you can set its starting attributes. Methods are functions defined in the class body; when you call `p.move(1)`, Python passes the instance itself as the first argument, which by convention is named `self`.

```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x          # instance variables: unique to each Point
        self.y = y

    def move(self, dx):
        self.x += dx

p = Point(1, 2)
p.move(3)                   # same as Point.move(p, 3)
print(p.x, p.y)             # 4 2
```

Put per-object data on `self` inside `__init__`. Variables written directly in the class body are **class variables**, shared by every instance — fine for constants, but a shared mutable list or dict is a classic bug. Validate inputs in `__init__` (raise `ValueError` for impossible values) so an object can never start in a broken state.
keyIdeas: Calling a class creates an instance; `__init__` sets it up.
Instance variables (on `self`) are per object; class variables are shared.
Validate in `__init__` so objects start valid.

workedExample.problem: Model a `Temperature` with a `celsius` attribute, a `fahrenheit()` method, and a rule that values below absolute zero (-273.15 °C) raise `ValueError`.
steps: Store the reading on the instance in `__init__`: `self.celsius = celsius`.
Check the rule before storing: `if celsius < -273.15: raise ValueError(...)`.
Add a method that uses `self`: `return self.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32`.
Create two instances to confirm they do not share state.

pitfalls: Forgetting `self` in a method definition (`def area():`), which raises `TypeError` when called on an instance.
Defining `items = []` in the class body: every instance shares that one list.
Writing `x = value` instead of `self.x = value` in `__init__`, which creates a local variable that disappears.

citations.quote: When a class defines an __init__() method, class instantiation automatically invokes __init__() for the newly created class instance.
the special thing about methods is that the instance object is passed as the first argument of the function. In our example, the call x.f() is exactly equivalent to MyClass.f(x).
Generally speaking, instance variables are for data unique to each instance and class variables are for attributes and methods shared by all instances of the class
shared data can have possibly surprising effects involving mutable objects such as lists and dictionaries.
